778.title: His family carried the dead cattle
778.word: His family carried the dead catt
778.hook: Ravidas sings that his family carried dead animals near Benares, yet great men bow to him now (Malar, Ravidas, ang 1293)
778.howItsDone: Sikhs hear these hymns of Ravidas in the gurdwara as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Sikh ideal of kirat karni, honest work, honors labor of every kind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who but You: the king's canopy held over a leather-worker's head, and Ravidas giving the credit away. Who did you lift, and did anyone notice? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

Before dawn, a truck stops outside, and someone you'll never meet lifts your trash and carries it off. A worker in a hospital basement washes what nobody wants to wash. Somewhere, a person handles the dead, so the rest of us don't have to. These jobs are easy to notice only by their absence: the day they aren't done. In Raag Malar, Ravidas starts a hymn by addressing the whole town and naming his family's work out loud. Not hinting at it. Naming it.
screen: `THE TRUCK BEFORE DAWN.` → `JOBS WE KNOW BY THEIR ABSENCE.` → `RAVIDAS NAMES HIS FAMILY'S WORK.`

segments.voice: The two hymns sit side by side on Ang 1293 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Four days ago we heard the second one, with the learned bowing. Today, start with the first. It opens, in paraphrase: people of the town, my caste is well known; it is the leather-workers' caste. And in my heart I hold the Lord's virtues. Then Ravidas reaches for a picture from a scribe's desk. In paraphrase: the palm tree is counted impure, and so is the paper made from its leaves. But when the Lord's praise is written on that paper, people bow before it and worship it. Hear what that does. The material doesn't change. The leaf still comes from the tree the town looked down on. What's written on it changes how it's treated. Ravidas sets himself right there: the same family, the same trade, and the Name written into him. Then the second hymn adds one small word that carries a lot: still. His relatives, he says, still go around Benares hauling away dead cattle. He doesn't say they used to, or that he got out. So the honor can't be explained by escape. Brahmins of careful conduct bow before him anyway, and he calls himself the servant of the Lord's servants. In that same hymn he names Kabir too, beside his own family's background, as if to say: the Lord keeps doing this. Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't ask to be reclassified. He doesn't say the work was beneath him. Sikh teaching has a name for honest work: kirat karni, earning by your own labor. So the line today, every job is holy, isn't Ravidas's exact phrase. It's what his song does. It names a job the town shrank from at the top of the hymn, and doesn't apologize.
screen: `PEOPLE OF THE TOWN, MY CASTE IS KNOWN.` · `PALM-LEAF PAPER, BOWED TO WHEN IT HOLDS PRAISE.` · `STILL HAULING DEAD CATTLE IN BENARES.` · then, large: `NO APOLOGY FOR THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: respect one dirty job. Use the sit to find one. Trace something you touched today back to the hands that dealt with its mess: the drain, the bin, the floor, the laundry, the shoes. Let one worker come to mind, even without a face. Stay with them a few breaths, without pity, the way Ravidas stays with his family's work. Then choose one way to show respect today: a thank-you, a clean handover, a tip, a greeting by name. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
His family carried the dead cattle. Ravidas, in Raag Malar, naming his family's trade before the whole town, and setting the bowing of the learned right beside it.
screen: `HIS FAMILY CARRIED THE DEAD CATTLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every job is holy. Today, when you meet someone doing the work nobody wants, look up, and say thank you like you mean it. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

779.title: Ravidas close
779.hook: Ravidas is honored by Sikhs, and by the Ravidassia community, who hold him especially dear
779.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Ravidas's hymns in the gurdwara as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, while the Ravidassia community honors him as Guru Ravidas in its own gatherings and celebrates his birthday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, his family carried the dead cattle: Ravidas naming his family's trade to the whole town, and the learned bowing anyway. Whose dirty job did you thank? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

Two buildings, maybe on the same street. In one, a gurdwara, Sikhs sing a hymn of Ravidas from the Guru Granth Sahib. In the other, members of the Ravidassia community gather under his picture and call him Guru Ravidas. Same man. Same songs. Two communities who honor him, each in its own way. Today we close the Ravidas days by looking at who keeps his song, and at what it means to honor a saint who is someone else's too.
screen: `TWO BUILDINGS, ONE NAME.` → `SIKHS SING HIS HYMNS.` → `THE RAVIDASSIA CALL HIM GURU.`

segments.voice: First, look back at what we've heard this week and last. The shoemaker of Benares, a leather-worker whose family were counted low. Begampura, his city without sorrow, with no tax and no fear, where all walk free. Sandalwood and castor: the plain plant made fragrant by standing close. Who but You: the king's canopy over his head. And yesterday, his family still hauling dead cattle while the learned bow. Five pictures, one voice. Now, who keeps that voice? For Sikhs, Ravidas is a Bhagat, a devotee, and his hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib. In the gurdwara they're sung with the same reverence as the Gurus' own words, and when they're read, the whole book is honored, not one author over another. For the Ravidassia community, Ravidas is their Guru, and he stands at the center. Ravidassia communities have their own places of worship, and his birthday is a great day for them. The two communities share a great deal and differ on some things, and each tells its own story about how they relate. This path won't settle that, and doesn't need to. What it can say is that the songs themselves don't belong to one fence. Begampura is a city where all walk free. That's a song that keeps opening the gate. And one plain fact stands: the man whose touch his town called polluting is now honored by more than one community, and they don't all honor him in the same words. His song is big enough for that.
screen: `FIVE PICTURES, ONE VOICE.` · `FOR SIKHS: A BHAGAT IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · `FOR THE RAVIDASSIA: THEIR GURU.` · then, large: `A SONG BIGGER THAN ONE FENCE.`

segments.voice: The practice: honor someone else's saint. Use the sit to bring to mind a holy figure who belongs to someone you know, but isn't yours, or isn't yours in the same way. A coworker's saint, a friend's teacher, a neighbor's guru. Hold their name with respect, the way you'd want yours held. If you know nothing about them, let that be the honest starting place, and decide to ask. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Ravidas close. The leather-worker of Benares: a Bhagat in the Guru Granth Sahib for Sikhs, Guru Ravidas for the Ravidassia, and a song big enough for both.
Your line: his song for all. Today, ask one person about a saint or teacher they love, and listen to the whole answer without adding yours. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

what a scholar hears: one body of songs, kept by more than one community, each with its own account of how they're related.

780.title: Trilochan: the last thought
780.hook: what we think of at the very end shapes where we go (Gujri, Trilochan, ang 526)
780.howItsDone: Trilochan's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs traditionally end the day with Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and simran, remembering the Name before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ravidas close: one leather-worker's songs, kept by Sikhs and by the Ravidassia. Your line was his song for all. Whose saint did you ask about? Day seven hundred eighty.

What was on your mind just before you fell asleep last night? A bill. A message you shouldn't have sent. Tomorrow's meeting. A face. Sometimes that thought is still there in the morning. Three days ago Ravidas named Trilochan among the devotees the Lord carried across. Today Trilochan gets his own hymn, and it's about that last thought, stretched to its limit: not the last thought before sleep, but the last one at the very end of a life.
screen: `THE THOUGHT BEFORE SLEEP.` → `STILL THERE IN THE MORNING.` → `TRILOCHAN: THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Gujri, on Ang 526 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Its refrain, the line it keeps coming back to, is a plea to a sister, in paraphrase: O sister, don't forget the Name of Gobind. Then Trilochan builds a ladder of pictures, all with the same frame. At the last moment, whoever thinks of wealth, and dies in that thought, is born again and again as a serpent. Coiled around the treasure, you might say. Whoever, at the end, thinks of sons and family, is born as a pig, nosing among a crowd of young. Whoever thinks of mansions dies and wanders like a ghost, haunting the halls. Each picture is the thought made into a body. In the hymn, what a person holds onto at the end, they become. And then the last verse turns. At the last moment, whoever thinks of the Lord and dies in that thought is set free, and the Lord, the hymn says, dwells in that heart. The hymn is a warning. Many readers also hear something practical in it: the thought that shows up at the end is likely the one that's been showing up all along, at red lights, in the shower, at two in the morning. That's why the refrain isn't about dying. It's about not forgetting, today. In the Sikh telling, the Name is remembered through simran, steady remembrance. Trilochan's pictures are strange, even a little grim. But the plea underneath is gentle: sister, don't forget.
screen: `O SISTER, DON'T FORGET THE NAME.` · `WEALTH, FAMILY, MANSIONS: THE THOUGHT BECOMES A BODY.` · `THE LORD AT THE END: SET FREE.` · then, large: `THE LAST THOUGHT IS PRACTICED NOW.`

segments.voice: The practice: end today with a good thought. Use the sit to choose it now, while it's easy. Something true and good: a face you love, a line you've learned on this path, a moment you're grateful for, or, if you pray, the Name. Say it to yourself slowly, until it's short enough to find in the dark. Then decide where it goes tonight: the last thing before your head meets the pillow. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Trilochan. The Bhagat of Raag Gujri whose refrain is a plea to a sister: don't forget the Name, because the last thought is made of all the others.
Your line: the last thought. Tonight, put your chosen thought last, and see whether it's still there when you wake. Day seven hundred eighty.

screen: `DAY 780 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BENI: THE STAGES OF LIFE.`

781.title: Beni: the stages of life
781.hook: Beni traces a life from the womb to old age, forgetting the Lord at each stage (Sri Rag, Beni, ang 93)
781.howItsDone: Beni's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching speaks of jivan mukti, being free while still alive, through remembering the Name in everyday life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trilochan: the last thought, and the plea to a sister not to forget the Name. What did you put last before sleep, and was it there this morning? Day seven hundred eighty-one.

A box of family photos, tipped out on a table. A baby in a hospital blanket. A kid with a scraped knee and a grin. A teenager trying hard to look bored. A wedding. A gray head bent over a grandchild. Shuffle them back into order and you have a whole life in a few minutes. Beni, one of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib, does exactly that in a hymn. He lays out the snapshots of a life, from the womb to old age. And in every one, something is missing.
screen: `A BOX OF PHOTOS ON THE TABLE.` → `A WHOLE LIFE IN ORDER.` → `IN EVERY ONE, SOMETHING MISSING.`

segments.voice: Beni's hymn is in Sri Raag, on Ang 93. He starts somewhere surprising: before birth. In paraphrase: O man, when you were in the womb, upside down, you were absorbed in remembering; you had no pride in your body. Then you were born, and you forgot. Next picture: childhood. The child is caught up in play and sweets, and the Lord slips from mind. Then youth: the body is strong, the eye wanders after pleasure and money, and the person grows proud. Then old age: the hair goes white, the body weakens, and there's regret, but now it's hard to change course. Each stage has its own reason to forget. The child is too busy. The young adult is too sure. The old one is too tired. Beni isn't mocking any of them. He's showing that forgetting doesn't belong to one bad season of life. It comes along to every one. Then he signs off with a hard question, in paraphrase: says Beni, listen, devotees, who has ever found liberation after death? That's the turn. If freedom doesn't come after death, it has to come in one of these photos. Sikh teaching speaks of being free while still alive, here, in the middle of an ordinary life. So the hymn isn't really about the box of pictures. It's about the one you're in right now: the stage you're standing in, with its own reason to forget. Read that way, Beni's question points to the stage you're in as the place to remember.
screen: `IN THE WOMB, REMEMBERING.` · `CHILD, YOUTH, OLD AGE: EACH ONE FORGETS.` · `WHO IS FREED AFTER DEATH?` · then, large: `THE STAGE YOU'RE IN NOW.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember at your stage. Use the sit to find yourself in Beni's photos. Which one are you standing in: busy like the child, sure like the young, tired like the old, or somewhere between? Name your stage's own reason to forget, honestly and without blame. Then pick one small moment in today's actual schedule, the commute, the dishes, the pause before sleep, and make it the moment you remember. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Beni. The Bhagat of Sri Raag who lays out a life from the womb to old age, finds forgetting in every stage, and asks who was ever freed after death.
Your line: remember at every stage. Today, when your chosen moment comes, stop for one breath and remember, right there in the stage you're in. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

782.title: Dhanna the farmer
782.hook: Dhanna prays plainly for flour, lentils, ghee, a cow and a good wife (Dhanasri, Dhanna, ang 695)
782.howItsDone: Dhanna's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bring ordinary needs as well as spiritual ones into ardas, the standing prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Beni: the photos of a life, forgetting in every one. Your line was remember at every stage. Did your chosen moment come, and did you stop? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

O Gopal, I'm a beggar at Your door. That's how one hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib begins, in paraphrase, and what follows sounds less like poetry than a shopping list. Between hymns about the soul and the Infinite, there it sits. It belongs to Dhanna, a farmer, and it's addressed straight to God. He doesn't dress it up or explain himself. He stands at the door and asks for groceries.
screen: `O GOPAL, A BEGGAR AT YOUR DOOR.` → `BETWEEN HYMNS OF THE SOUL, A LIST.` → `DHANNA ASKS FOR GROCERIES.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 695. It opens with the word aarta. Some read it as one in need, a beggar at the door; others hear in it aarti, an offering of worship. In paraphrase: O Gopal, Sustainer of the world, I'm a beggar at Your door; You take care of the work of those who are devoted to You. Then comes the list. Lentils, flour and ghee, so my heart can be content each day. Shoes, and good clothes. Grain. A cow and a buffalo that give milk. A fine horse. And a good wife to keep the home. The last line: your servant Dhanna asks for these. That's it. No apology, no explanation that what he really wants is something higher. Notice what kind of things they are. Food for the table. Something on the feet. Animals that keep a farm alive. A partner. It's the list of a working household, said out loud to the Lord as if the Lord were the one who could be asked. And the hymn stands in the Guru's book, beside songs of longing for the Lord. Why does that matter? Because some people feel a prayer has to be cleaned up before it's said: made noble, made about other people, the part about rent hidden. Dhanna's hymn sits there quietly saying the plain thing is allowed. Trust shows up in the asking. Tradition tells other stories about Dhanna, about a stone and a simple farmer's faith, and we'll leave those for another day. Today it's just the list, and the man who wasn't embarrassed to say it to God.
screen: `A BEGGAR AT YOUR DOOR, GOPAL.` · `LENTILS, FLOUR, GHEE, SHOES, A COW.` · `KEPT IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · then, large: `THE PLAIN THING IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for a plain thing, if you pray. If you don't, simply name one. Use the sit to find it: not the noblest need you have, the most ordinary one. Groceries for the week. A night of sleep. A car that starts. A kind word at work. Say it plainly, without decorating it. If you pray, offer it as Dhanna did, as someone asking at a door. If you don't, hold it honestly as a need. You can also say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Dhanna the farmer. The Bhagat of Raag Dhanasri who asked the Lord for lentils, flour, ghee, shoes, a cow and a good wife, and whose list sits in the Guru's book.
Your line: plain prayers count. Today, when a small need shows up, don't wave it away; name it plainly, once. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

783.title: Sain the barber
783.hook: Sain's aarti offers incense, lamp and ghee, then his whole self (Dhanasri, Sain, ang 695)
783.howItsDone: Sain's aarti is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching counts honest work, kirat, as part of a devoted life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhanna the farmer: lentils, flour, ghee and a cow, asked for plainly at the Lord's door. Your line was plain prayers count. What plain thing did you name? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

How close do you let a stranger come to your face with a blade? A barber's day is made of small, careful movements an inch from someone's throat. Trust is the whole job. Tradition remembers Sain as a barber, and on the same page of the Guru Granth Sahib as Dhanna's grocery list, he left a hymn of worship. It's an aarti: the lamp ceremony, with incense and flame. But by the end, the thing he's offering isn't on the tray.
screen: `A BLADE NEAR THE FACE.` → `A BARBER'S CAREFUL HANDS.` → `AN AARTI ON THE SAME PAGE.`

segments.voice: Aarti, in Indian worship, is the waving of a lamp before the divine, often with incense and a lamp fed with ghee, clarified butter. Sain's hymn, in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695, opens right there. In paraphrase: with incense, lamp and ghee I make ready the aarti. And then, immediately, the next breath: I am a sacrifice to the Lord. Vaarne jaau, in the Gurmukhi: I give myself over. That's the turn the whole hymn hangs on. The tray is set, but the offering is the person holding it. The refrain is pure celebration, in paraphrase: joy to the Lord, joy every day to the Sovereign King. Then Sain looks at the lamp again. The finest lamp, the purest wick, he sings, and then turns to the Lord: You are the Immaculate One. As if the true flame isn't the one in his hand. Then a surprise: Sain names a teacher. Ramanand, he says, knows the devotion of the Lord, and speaks of the Lord as perfect, supreme bliss. We'll meet Ramanand's own hymn in a few days. And the close: Sain says, worship the Lord, the supreme bliss, who carries you across the frightening sea. Tradition tells a story about Sain, retold by the Sikh poet Bhai Gurdas: that once he stayed so long with holy people that he missed his duty at the king's court, and the Lord came in his form and served the king in his place. Whatever you make of the story, it fits the hymn: the barber's work and the barber's worship are one offering.
screen: `INCENSE, LAMP AND GHEE.` · `VAARNE JAAU: I GIVE MYSELF.` · `YOU ARE THE TRUE FLAME.` · then, large: `THE WORK AND THE WORSHIP, ONE OFFERING.`

segments.voice: The practice: offer your work today. Use the sit to set your own tray. What will your hands do today? Emails, meals, a shift, a diaper, a spreadsheet, a classroom. Picture the tools of it the way Sain had scissors and comb. Then, quietly, decide to offer the work itself, done carefully, as your aarti, whether you call it that or not. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sain the barber. The Bhagat of Raag Dhanasri who set out incense, lamp and ghee for the aarti, then offered himself, and named his teacher Ramanand.
Your line: the barber's aarti. Today, pick one task you'd rather rush, and do it with a barber's careful hands, as an offering. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: Pipa the king
784.hook: a king turned devotee sings that the body itself is the temple (Dhanasri, Pipa, ang 695)
784.howItsDone: Pipa's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, on the same page as the hymns of Dhanna and Sain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sain the barber: incense, lamp and ghee, and then himself as the offering. Your line was the barber's aarti. Which task did you do with careful hands? Day seven hundred eighty-four.

A king has everything a temple needs: money for the marble, priests on the payroll, gold for the lamps. Tradition says Pipa was a king like that, who left his throne to follow the path of devotion. So when a man like that sings about where God is worshipped, you might expect a grand building. Instead, on the same page as Dhanna and Sain, Pipa points to something much closer. It's been with you all day. It's breathing right now.
screen: `MARBLE, PRIESTS, GOLD LAMPS.` → `A KING WHO LEFT THE THRONE.` → `HE POINTS SOMEWHERE CLOSER.`

segments.voice: Pipa's hymn is in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 695. Its key word is kaaiaa, the body. In paraphrase, it opens: the body is the deity, the body is the temple, the body is the pilgrim. Within the body are the incense, the lamp and the offerings of food. Within the body are the leaves laid down in worship. Hear it next to yesterday. Sain set out incense, lamp and ghee on the tray, then offered himself. Pipa takes the whole tray and moves it inside. The temple, the pilgrim walking to it, the lamp, the offering: all of it is found in the body. Then the story of a search. In paraphrase: I searched through many realms, and found the treasures within the body. Nothing comes and nothing goes. And then a line worth holding onto: what is in the universe is in the body; whoever searches, finds. The hymn closes: Pipa prays, the supreme essence is there, and the True Guru reveals it. Notice two things. First, this isn't about the body as something to perfect or show off. It's about the body as the place where the sacred is met, the ordinary one, tired or sick or young or old. Second, it isn't a do-it-yourself map. Pipa ends with the True Guru, the one who shows you what was there all along. A king who could have paid for any temple, saying: the temple was here.
screen: `KAAIAA: THE BODY.` · `DEITY, TEMPLE, PILGRIM, LAMP: ALL WITHIN.` · `WHAT'S IN THE UNIVERSE IS IN THE BODY.` · then, large: `THE TRUE GURU SHOWS IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: honor your body as a temple. Not by judging it. Use the sit to walk through it gently, the way a pilgrim walks into a holy place. The feet that carried you here. The hands that worked. The chest rising and falling. Whatever aches, let it be part of the temple too. Then choose one small act of honor for later today: water, rest, a walk, a kind word to yourself in the mirror. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Pipa the king. The king turned devotee who sang in Raag Dhanasri that the body is the deity, the temple and the pilgrim, and the True Guru shows what's inside.

Your line: the body is the temple. This week went from dead cattle to a farmer's list, a barber's lamp and now a king's temple. Close it with your one act of honor today. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

myth: Pipa's hymn is about building a grand temple
it says the body itself is the deity, the temple and the pilgrim.
Pipa says anyone can find it alone, no guide needed
the hymn closes: the True Guru reveals the supreme essence.
Pipa's hymn is on the same page as Sain's and Dhanna's
all three are in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695.

fork.setup: you're Pipa, and you've searched through many realms looking for the treasure. where do you find it?
options: in a far pilgrimage city.
in the royal treasury you left.
within the body.
fork.reveal: within the body, he sings: what is in the universe is in the body, and whoever searches, finds.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the body, the word Pipa's hymn turns into a temple (Ang 695).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'the body is a temple' means eat well and exercise.
what it means: the body is where the sacred is met: deity, temple, pilgrim and offering, all within.
what a scholar hears: the hymn ends on the True Guru, so the inward search is guided, not do-it-yourself.

sources.ref: Dhanasri, Pipa (kaayau devaa kaaiau deval), Ang 695
